### TL;DR
- **Hosted Linux runners may now run on AWS as well as Azure.** Allowlists or Entra Conditional Access policies that only permit Azure or Microsoft ranges can break workflows. The rollout is already underway, so update allowlists now. ([changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-28-github-actions-adds-multi-cloud-compute-to-improve-reliability))
- **Actions workflow lockfiles are generally available.** This includes Dependabot integration and a **Require lockfile** policy. Lockfiles cover step-level actions only, not job-level reusable workflows. ([changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-28-github-actions-workflow-lockfiles-are-generally-available), [docs](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/administer/control-workflow-execution))
- **GitHub Agentic Workflows are generally available.** Agents run inside Actions with read-only defaults, a sandbox and firewall, safe outputs and threat detection. ([changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-28-github-agentic-workflows-generally-available))
- **Several new secret, code and supply-chain security features shipped:**
  - Public monitoring is generally available.
  - AI-based push protection, AI Scan for repositories, code scanning for AI applications and Dependabot reachability analysis are in public preview.

### Action required
No hard deadlines or dates were announced. The following changes need action because they are rolling out now or can block runs:
- **Update network allowlists for multi-cloud runners.**
  - **Who is affected:** Standard 2-core and 4-core Linux runners, and compatible larger runners without specialized configurations, can run on AWS. Windows runners and runners with private networking are not affected.
  - **When it applies:** It is automatic on Free, Pro and Team plans. Enterprise Cloud customers opt in under *Enterprise settings > Actions > Hosted compute cloud providers*.
  - **What to do:** Sync allowlists with the `actions` array from `GET https://api.github.com/meta` instead of using cloud-provider-specific ranges.
  - **Why:** Azure-only or Microsoft-only rules can block connections or authentication, including Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policies.
  - Sources: [changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-28-github-actions-adds-multi-cloud-compute-to-improve-reliability), [IP docs](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/runners/github-hosted-runners)
- **Check for Azure SDK `DefaultAzureCredential` failures on multi-cloud runners.**
  - **Symptom:** Authentication can fail even after `azure/login` succeeds, with a `ManagedIdentityCredential ... 401` error.
  - **Cause:** AWS EC2 and Azure use the same instance metadata address, `169.254.169.254`. Some Azure Identity SDKs misread the EC2 response and stop the credential chain.
  - **Fix:** Use `AzureCLICredential` explicitly. For Go with `azidentity` 1.11.0 or later, set `AZURE_TOKEN_CREDENTIALS: AzureCLICredential` on the application step.
  - Source: [troubleshooting docs](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/troubleshoot-workflows)
- **Prepare repositories before enforcing Require lockfile.**
  - Setting the policy to *Active* blocks targeted workflows that aren't onboarded to a lockfile.
  - It also blocks a caller whose reusable workflow isn't onboarded in that workflow's own repository.
  - Onboard shared-workflow repositories first and do a staged rollout.
  - Sources: [control execution](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/administer/control-workflow-execution), [enforce lockfiles](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/administer/enforce-workflow-lockfiles)

### Security improvements
- **Workflow lockfiles (GA)**
  - `gh actions-lock` generates `.github/workflows/actions.lock`, which pins actions and their transitive dependencies to the commits you locked.
  - Other GA capabilities:
    - Workflows can be onboarded one at a time.
    - Dependabot regenerates the matching lockfile entry in its version-update pull requests.
    - The Require lockfile policy is available at enterprise, organization and repository level.
    - A stale-lockfile check can run in CI.
  - Lockfiles don't judge whether a dependency is safe, so review dependencies before locking them.
  - Source: [changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-28-github-actions-workflow-lockfiles-are-generally-available)
- **GitHub Agentic Workflows (GA)**
  - Natural-language Markdown workflows compile to standard Actions YAML and reuse your runner groups and policies.
  - Built-in safeguards:
    - Agents respect integrity filter rules and run with read-only permissions by default.
    - Agents run in a sandboxed container behind the Agent Workflow Firewall.
    - Outputs are validated through safe outputs, and a threat detection job scans proposed changes.
  - New since public preview:
    - Isolation in Cloud Hypervisor or NVX micro-VMs.
    - Enclaves that prevent data leaks in cross-repository workflows.
    - Support for self-hosted ARC runners with Docker-in-Docker.
  - Source: [changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-28-github-agentic-workflows-generally-available)
- **Push protection for AI-detected secrets (public preview)**
  - A context-aware classifier blocks secrets that have no known format.
  - It is off by default and requires both AI-detected secrets and push protection to be enabled.
  - It consumes AI credits.
  - REST field: `secret_scanning_generic_secrets_push_protection`.
  - Source: [changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-28-push-protection-beyond-predefined-secret-patterns)
- **Public monitoring (GA)**
  - Alerts enterprises when their secrets leak anywhere in public GitHub content, including issues, pull request comments and gists.
  - Free for enterprises with GitHub Secret Protection.
  - Now supported on data residency, using verified-domain attribution only.
  - Source: [changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-28-public-monitoring-for-enterprises-generally-available)
- **AI Scan for repositories (public preview)**
  - On-demand agentic scan of the default branch in any language, with findings shown in the code scanning alert list.
  - Alerts don't auto-close when a fix is merged; rescan to close them.
  - Consumes Code Security AI credits.
  - Source: [changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-28-ai-scan-for-repositories-in-public-preview)
- **Code scanning for AI applications (public preview, GHAS)**
  - Scans pull requests for indirect prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure and excessive agency.
  - Source: [changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-28-code-scanning-for-ai-applications-in-public-preview)
- **Dependabot reachability analysis (public preview)**
  - Covers JavaScript and TypeScript on GitHub Enterprise Cloud.
  - Verdicts are Reachable, Potentially reachable, Unreachable or Reachability unavailable.
  - Runs in a managed Actions workflow on GitHub-hosted runners only, and is free during the preview.
  - Source: [changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-28-prioritize-dependabot-alerts-with-reachability-analysis)
- **Security extension for the GitHub Copilot app (public preview)**
  - Lets you browse, explain, fix and dismiss code scanning alerts, and run `/security-review` on local changes.
  - Fixes stay in your local working copy and are never committed or pushed automatically.
  - Source: [changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-28-security-extension-for-the-github-copilot-app)
- **Governance notes for Copilot features**
  - Shared Copilot Automations act as Copilot and are billed to the repository owner. In organization-owned repositories they require the "Allow use of Copilot cloud agent billed to the organization" policy. ([changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-28-build-shared-workflows-for-your-team-with-copilot-automations))
  - Copilot app computer use asks for approval before controlling an app and can be disabled through managed settings. ([changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-28-github-copilot-app-universe-releases))

### Docs changes worth reading
- **[GitHub-hosted runners (concepts)](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/runners/github-hosted-runners):** The cloud hosts section now describes the AWS and Azure multi-cloud pool and which runners are eligible.
- **[GitHub-hosted runners (reference)](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/runners/github-hosted-runners):** The statement that Ubuntu runners use Azure IP ranges was replaced with guidance to sync allowlists with the full `actions` IP array.
- **[Manage larger runners](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/manage-runners/larger-runners/manage-larger-runners):** The note that same-region Azure Storage traffic uses private Azure IPs now applies explicitly to Azure-hosted runner VMs only.
- **[Troubleshoot workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/troubleshoot-workflows):** A new "Azure SDK authentication failures" section covers the shared metadata-address problem and its workarounds.
- **[Larger runners](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/runners/larger-runners):** Billing changed. Larger runner costs can now draw from included compute usage on Team and Enterprise Cloud, where available; previously they were always billed per minute. Public repositories are still billed per minute.
- **Lockfile docs:**
  - [Concepts](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/workflow-dependency-lockfiles) and [how-to](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/secure-your-work/lock-workflow-dependencies) dropped their preview notes. They now state that a reusable workflow's dependencies are covered only by the lockfile in its own repository.
  - [Enforce lockfiles](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/administer/enforce-workflow-lockfiles) notes that anyone with write access can create a lockfile, so teams can onboard before central enforcement.
- **[Push protection concepts](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/secret-security/push-protection) and [Enable AI push protection](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/how-tos/secure-your-secrets/prevent-future-leaks/enable-ai-push-protection) (new):**
  - Blocked secret types are now organized by category, including partner and generic patterns.
  - The new page covers prerequisites and AI credit billing.
  - The [supported patterns table](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/reference/secret-security/supported-secret-scanning-patterns) now lists push protection for the AI-detected column, where available.
- **Public monitoring docs ([concepts](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/secret-security/public-monitoring), [enable](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/how-tos/secure-at-scale/configure-enterprise-security/manage-your-coverage/enabling-public-monitoring-for-your-enterprise), [alerts](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/how-tos/view-and-interpret-data/analyze-organization-data/viewing-public-monitoring-alerts)):**
  - Preview notes were removed and data residency is now supported.
  - Enterprise security managers can now enable the feature and view alerts.
  - A triage section was added to the alerts page.
- **AI Scan docs:**
  - New [AI Scan overview](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/code-scanning/ai-scan) explains the three separately controlled features: AI Scan for repositories, AI Scan for pull requests, and scanning for AI applications.
  - New pages cover [AI Scan for repositories](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/code-scanning/ai-scan-for-repositories), [managing AI Scan alerts](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/how-tos/manage-security-alerts/manage-code-scanning-alerts/viewing-and-managing-ai-scan-alerts) and [AI applications scanning](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/code-scanning/ai-applications-scanning-for-pull-requests).
- **Reachability docs:** New pages [About reachability analysis](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/supply-chain-security/about-reachability-analysis-for-dependabot-alerts) and [Configure reachability analysis](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/how-tos/secure-your-supply-chain/secure-your-dependencies/configure-reachability-analysis). The changes also cover:
  - **Most important** sorting deprioritizes only alerts marked Unreachable. ([view alerts](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/how-tos/manage-security-alerts/manage-dependabot-alerts/view-dependabot-alerts))
  - A new `reachability:` filter is available in security overview. ([filters](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/reference/security-at-scale/overview-dashboard-filters))

changelog.title: Route and orchestrate models with GitHub Copilot Fusion
changelog.text: GitHub Copilot Fusion is generally available. Instead of picking a model for each task, choose Copilot Fusion and let Copilot intelligently route and orchestrate which models it uses for you. Copilot Fusion brings together Project HydraFusion’s multi-model orchestration and Copilot auto model selection’s fine-tuned model selection, leveraging the benefits of both to balance performance and cost efficiency. Since Project HydraFusion launched, we’ve improved its performance. In the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Copilot Fusion Max scored 60, within two points of Claude Code with Opus 5.5 Max. It delivered that result at about half the average API cost per task, using about half as many tokens and taking about 40% less time per task. Smarter choices for developers When you select Copilot Fusion in the model picker, you aren’t selecting a specific model. You’re choosing a system that routes and orchestrates models for each task. There’s no need to switch models during a task or decide which model suits each step. For each prompt, Copilot Fusion determines which models to use and how they work together, while you choose the right level of effort. To use it, select Copilot Fusion in the model picker, then choose the effort level. Fusion Standard: Prioritizes versatile models for everyday coding. Fusion High: Prioritizes capable models for challenging tasks and deeper reasoning. Fusion Max: Prioritizes the most capable models for the most demanding tasks and complex reasoning. Watch as Copilot Fusion analyzes each task and selects a model to complete it, orchestrating multiple models through the following workflows when needed. Single: One model solves the task directly. Cascade: An efficient model drafts a response. A quality check determines whether to accept it or escalate to a stronger model. Critique: One model drafts an initial response, another model reviews it, and the original model revises. More control for administrators Administrators control which models Copilot Fusion can use and whether Copilot Fusion is the default. Copilot Fusion only uses the models that are enabled in your enterprise and organization model policies . Enterprise administrators can view what models Copilot Fusion picks from, independently set each model’s effective policy state, and disable models for Copilot Fusion without disabling the model for everyone. See Manage availability of default models . Administrators can set Copilot Fusion, at any effort level, as the default model for Copilot users with Enterprise managed settings. To configure settings, see Enterprise managed settings . “GitHub Copilot Fusion Standard has improved token efficiency across AT&T by automatically selecting the right model for the task, reducing unnecessary spend and preserving capacity for higher-value work. Previously, developers would often choose a more powerful model for a complex task and forget to switch back for everyday activities. Copilot Fusion eliminates that friction, optimizing model selection without requiring developers to manage it themselves. We’ve also seen its decision-making improve over time, giving developers greater confidence to focus on their work while Copilot handles model selection.” Hari Pokhrel, Principal Software Engineer, AT&T Billing When you use Copilot Fusion you’re billed for each model it uses, at each model’s standard rate. For a limited time, users on paid Copilot plans will receive a 30% discount on model costs when using Copilot Fusion. Get started Copilot Fusion is available on all Copilot plans in Visual Studio Code, the GitHub Copilot app, GitHub Copilot CLI, and JetBrains IDEs. Support for additional clients is coming soon. Update your client to try it out. Open the model picker, select Copilot Fusion , and choose an effort level. Note for research preview participants: if you previously enabled auto, HydraFusion, or HydraFusion Max, your selections will automatically transition to the corresponding Copilot Fusion eff

changelog.title: GitHub Copilot app, Universe releases
changelog.text: Work doesn’t always fit in a single repository or session. A feature can span several repositories. A launch plan can pull in specs, designs, and assets without touching a repository at all. Projects in the GitHub Copilot app give that work one home, with its context, agents, and results together. Copilot coordinates the work in the background and checks in when it needs you. Give Copilot a goal Start a project, describe what you want to get done, and add the context Copilot needs (e.g., repositories, design mocks, Slack threads, or notes from a design meeting). Choose the models and tools for the job. Copilot runs as many agents as the work needs and brings back results (e.g., pull requests) for your review. Use project automations for repeatable tasks, such as creating a new promo video whenever a feature lands. For a focused task in a single repository, you can still start a session directly from that repository. Copilot Projects are now in public preview. You can learn more in the projects documentation . Handle the work around your code Use context from connected tools such as Slack and Figma to research a request, draft a specification, or work through a design alongside your code. You can also generate and edit images using natural language in chat. Let Copilot work with your desktop apps Ask Copilot to work through tasks in your desktop apps, such as an expense-report workflow. Computer use—in public preview on macOS and Windows—lets Copilot read app content, click controls, enter or edit text, and navigate across apps, including those without an API, command-line interface, or MCP integration. Copilot asks for your approval before controlling an app, and your organization can disable the feature through managed settings. To get started, open Settings > Computer Use and turn on Enable Computer Use . On macOS, grant the required Accessibility and Screen Recording permissions. For more information, see the computer use documentation . Get started Download or update the GitHub Copilot app and join the discussion in GitHub Community . The post GitHub Copilot app, Universe releases appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

changelog.title: Security extension for the GitHub Copilot app
changelog.text: You can now work through your repository’s GitHub code scanning alerts without leaving the GitHub Copilot app. The new GitHub security extension, now in public preview, lets you find the alerts that matter most and ask Copilot to explain or help fix them. Until now, fixing a code scanning alert meant switching between the alert on github.com and the code in your editor. With the security extension, you can move from finding an alert to fixing it in one place. Fix the alerts already in your code If you already run code scanning on your repository, the security extension shows its open code scanning alerts: Browse every open code scanning alert, ordered by severity, and use search and filters to narrow the list. Open an alert to see its details and the affected code. You can open the full alert page on github.com when you need more context. Select one or more alerts and ask Copilot to Explain or Fix them. Copilot only makes fixes in your local working copy and doesn’t commit or push anything. This way you can review and iterate on the changes in the app and push when you’re ready. See linked pull requests on an alert so you know whether someone is already working on a fix. Dismiss alerts you don’t plan to fix. If your organization uses delegated alert dismissal, the extension sends your dismissal for approval. Catch new issues before you open a pull request Run /security-review on your current changes and see those findings next to your existing alerts. The extension tells you when your code has changed since the last review so you know when to run it again. You can also ask Copilot about your alerts in chat. Copilot uses the security extension’s tools in the same way as any other tool, following your tool permission settings. Get started To install the security extension: In your terminal run copilot plugin install github-security@awesome-copilot . In the GitHub Copilot app, click Customize , search for github-security , then click + Install . The extension is automatically enabled, and you can open the Security canvas from a session for your repository. The Explain , Fix , and /security-review actions use the model you’ve selected in the app and consume AI credits in the same way as any other prompt. Browsing and dismissing alerts don’t use AI. The security extension is in public preview on github.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. GitHub Enterprise Server isn’t supported. With any Copilot plan: You can install the extension and run /security-review on your local changes. For Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise, an administrator needs to enable the GitHub Copilot app policy, and can use enterprise managed settings to control which plugins developers can install. With code scanning: You can see, fix, and dismiss existing alerts for repositories where code scanning is enabled and you have permission to view the alerts. Private repositories need GitHub Code Security for this. Learn more in the security extension documentation and join the discussion in GitHub Community . The post Security extension for the GitHub Copilot app appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

changelog.title: GitHub intelligence puts your code, context, and history to work
changelog.text: Agents should understand more than your codebase—they should understand how your team works. Your preferences, repository conventions, skills, and custom instructions guide how changes should be made, while code in related repositories can show how the pieces fit together. Without that context, agents spend time rediscovering knowledge and can miss your team’s conventions. GitHub intelligence is the context and learning layer sourced from the graph of GitHub data. It makes this data useful to agents, helping them remember how you work, keep that guidance current, and find the code and development history relevant to the next task. The goal is for agents to build on what you and your team already know, rather than treating every session as a fresh start. That is the advantage of building where your team’s work already lives. A repository memory can capture why an edge case matters and which test covers it. GitHub intelligence allows agents to use that context, with controls over what they can access. Three capabilities bring this into your workflow: Memory carries knowledge between sessions Dreaming keeps the context current Code search reaches beyond your checkout. Availability and settings vary by capability. Memory: Pick up where you left off GitHub Copilot Memory is now generally available on paid Copilot plans. Copilot can remember personal preferences and repository conventions across sessions and clients. Memories can be created in the Copilot app, Copilot CLI, VS Code, Copilot cloud agent, Copilot code review, Slack, Teams, and GitHub Mobile. You can tell Copilot, Remember to start my pull request descriptions with a TL;DR , and it can reuse that preference across Copilot experiences. Repository memories can capture the right test command or how your team expects Copilot to check its work, so you spend less time repeating guidance in each session. Copilot sessions autonomously generate and curate memories, learning from every interaction. Among the Copilot CLI sessions reviewed during the public preview where the agent used memory, 93% showed better adherence to developer preferences and 42% showed more efficient workflows attributed to the memories included in the session context. You can interact with memories in the Copilot app, Copilot CLI, and VS Code, or manage personal memories in your Copilot settings, where you can view or delete saved preferences . Dreaming: Continuous context improvement Copilot dreaming, now in public preview, reflects on past work to improve future agentic sessions. Three dream types are currently available: Personal memory curation customizes Copilot to your personal preferences by updating memories based on your agent conversations. Repository customization manages repository-scoped memories and proposes updates and improvements to existing skills and custom instruction files. Code review customization turns recurring accepted code-review feedback into guidance for Copilot code review. Dreaming can add, update, and remove personal and repository memories. Changes to checked-in skills and instructions are proposed in pull requests for your team to review. Dreaming is opt-in. Individual subscribers: Enable personal curation in your Copilot settings and repository dreams in each repository’s settings. See personal and repository setup . Organizations and enterprises: Administrators enable dreaming through Copilot policies . Enterprise administrators can delegate that choice to organization administrators. Repository dreams cover the repositories allowed by Copilot Memory’s repository access settings. Users must also enable personal dreaming in their own Copilot settings. Dream runs consume AI credits. See the dreaming documentation for prerequisites, setup, and costs . Code Search: Reach beyond your checkout Software projects rarely live in a single repository. changelog.title: Build shared workflows for your team with Copilot Automations
changelog.text: Shared Copilot Automations are rolling out, enabling teams to build and maintain AI-powered workflows together. With Copilot Automations, you can combine prompts, triggers, and tools to design workflows around the way your team works. Copilot runs autonomously in the cloud, using only the tools you’ve allowed. For example, you could create automations to: Reproduce bugs as soon as an issue is opened. Capture screenshots of the changes when a pull request is marked as ready. Automatically investigate production incidents as soon as they’re detected in your monitoring tool. Until now, automations have been personal, meaning only you could see and edit them, and they used your identity and AI credits. That works well for automating your own work, like drafting your standup updates, but not for workflows your whole team relies on. Shared automations let your team build and maintain those workflows together. How shared automations work Visible to your team : Everyone with read access to the repository can see a shared automation, and anyone with write access can edit it. Billed to the repository owner : AI credits are billed to the organization or user that owns the repository, rather than to the person who created the automation. Act as Copilot : Actions on GitHub are attributed to Copilot, rather than to any one user. Built to last : Shared automations belong to the repository, so they keep running if the person who created them leaves the team. Change history lets your team see how the tools, triggers, and prompt have evolved. For shared automations to run in an organization-owned repository, an administrator must enable the “Allow use of Copilot cloud agent billed to the organization” policy. Create a shared automation When you create an automation on github.com, the GitHub Copilot app , or Visual Studio Code, choose Shared under Type . You can’t change an automation’s type after you create it. To learn more, see personal and shared automations . Shared Copilot Automations are rolling out to users on Copilot Pro, Pro+, Max, Business, and Enterprise plans. Availability may vary as the rollout progresses. Once available, you can create automations in any repository where you have write access. Join the discussion within GitHub Community . The post Build shared workflows for your team with Copilot Automations appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

changelog.title: Generate and edit images directly in Copilot
changelog.text: You can now generate and edit images using natural language in GitHub Copilot. When you ask for an image, your selected reasoning model calls a dedicated image-generation tool powered by GPT Image 2.5 Flare, previews the result inline, and saves it to your project. Previously, getting a visual asset while working in Copilot meant stepping away to a separate tool, describing what you needed again, generating it there, and manually bringing it back into your project. This update removes that context switch, so you can go from an idea to a usable image without breaking your flow. Describe an image conversationally in any Copilot chat session, whether you’re starting a new request or in the middle of a coding task. Copilot previews the generated image inline and saves it directly to your workspace. Organization and enterprise owners can turn off image generation by disabling the image generation model using Copilot model policies . You can opt in to a visible “Made with AI” watermark on images Copilot generates and edits. Watermarking is off by default. To try it, open a Copilot chat in VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, or Copilot CLI and describe the image you want. Image generation is in public preview for Copilot Pro, Copilot Pro+, Copilot Business, and Copilot Enterprise. It’s billed separately from your chat model, based on image tokens that count toward your plan’s AI credits. Join the discussion within GitHub Community . The post Generate and edit images directly in Copilot appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

changelog.title: GitHub Agentic Workflows generally available
changelog.text: GitHub Agentic Workflows , an open source project from GitHub Next, is now generally available. With agentic workflows, you can automate reasoning-based tasks like issue triage, CI failure analysis, documentation updates, and test writing by using coding agents inside GitHub Actions. Define your automation in natural language Markdown files, and GitHub Agentic Workflows compiles them into standard Actions YAML. Because these are GitHub Actions, they reuse your existing runner groups and policy constraints. You can use GitHub Copilot or bring your own coding agent to power each workflow. We’ve been rolling out our agentic developer workflows, and the results are measurable. One of our leads saved an estimated 29 hours a week on his development work alone. Across his team, measured velocity has more than doubled on average, and AI now authors 91% of the team’s commits. With these workflows, the team cut production errors from about 11,000 a day to under 1,000 and drove a technology migration end to end. One workflow takes a feature from requirements to implementation with validation evidence. Others keep our frameworks current and steadily raise code quality and test coverage. Because AI drives the process to completion, our engineers can run four or five efforts in parallel and stay focused on the bigger goals. Ben Alton – Senior manager, Strategy, Architecture & Innovation team at Accenture Built-in safeguards GitHub Agentic Workflows incorporates layered safeguards for your automation. Agents access GitHub content respecting the integrity filter rules, run with read-only permissions by default, and execute inside a sandboxed container behind the Agent Workflow Firewall . The outputs are validated through the safe outputs process, and a dedicated threat detection job scans all proposed changes before they are applied. Additional capabilities for general availability Highlights since the public preview include: Actions Runner Controller (ARC) and Docker-in-Docker support: Run agentic workflows on self-hosted ARC runners with Docker-in-Docker. Improved budget forecasting: gh aw forecast is no longer experimental. It now includes both threat detection credits and monthly ranges for a fuller picture of your AI credit spend. New models, engine choices, and workflows: The model inventory has been refreshed, model providers can be picked per workflow, and there are new workflow templates that can be added with gh aw add-wizard . Model routing: Workflows can use a model router that optimizes for task type and difficulty. Improved agent isolation: Agents can run in a Cloud Hypervisor or NVX micro-VM and prevent data leaks in cross-repository workflows with enclaves. See the GitHub Agentic Workflows release notes for the full list of changes. Get started Follow the quickstart guide to install the CLI extension and trigger your first workflow in minutes. Explore prebuilt workflows in GitHub Next’s agentics repository for ready-to-use examples covering triage, dependency management, code review, and reporting. GitHub Agentic Workflows is now generally available on github.com for GitHub Free, Team, and Enterprise. Using the default GitHub Copilot CLI engine to power a workflow requires a Copilot license. Learn more in the GitHub Agentic Workflows documentation , and join the conversation in the community discussion . The post GitHub Agentic Workflows generally available appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

changelog.title: GitHub Actions adds multi-cloud compute to improve reliability
changelog.text: We’re expanding the infrastructure behind GitHub-hosted runners so your workflows start faster and run more reliably, even during periods of peak demand. GitHub Actions now schedules eligible jobs across a broader, multi-cloud compute pool. This adds capacity, reduces capacity-related queue times, and improves service resilience. As part of this, eligible Linux jobs may run on Amazon Web Services (AWS) in addition to Microsoft Azure. Multi-cloud compute will be used for standard 2-core and 4-core Linux runners and compatible 2-core and 4-core larger runners without specialized configurations. This change does not apply to Windows runners or runners with private networking or other specialized configurations. For customers on GitHub Free, GitHub Pro, and GitHub Team, eligible runners will automatically use multi-cloud compute. Customers on GitHub Enterprise Cloud can opt in by going to Enterprise settings > Actions > Hosted compute cloud providers and enabling AWS compute. GitHub Actions automatically schedules eligible jobs across available cloud providers. Your existing runner labels and workflow syntax remain unchanged. Recommended action: Keep your network allowlists up to date To get the full benefit of expanded capacity, make sure any IP allowlists or network-based access policies your workflows rely on include all published GitHub Actions IP ranges. Runners in the expanded compute pool use additional outbound IP addresses, so policies that allow only Azure or Microsoft-owned ranges, including Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policies, can block connections or authentication from these runners. This is a rolling change, so we recommend updating your allowlists now, before your workflows begin running in the expanded compute pool. All GitHub Actions runner IP ranges, including the new ones, are published in the actions array returned by GET https://api.github.com/meta . We recommend keeping your allowlists in sync with this endpoint rather than relying on cloud-provider-specific ranges. See GitHub-hosted runner IP addresses for details. The post GitHub Actions adds multi-cloud compute to improve reliability appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

changelog.title: GitHub Actions workflow lockfiles are generally available
changelog.text: You can now use GitHub Actions workflow dependency lockfiles in general availability on GitHub Enterprise Cloud, GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency, Team, and Free plans. Lockfiles let you keep readable tag and branch references in your workflows while running the exact commits you locked, even if those references move. This release brings the capabilities introduced in the public preview to general availability: Lock your dependencies: Use the gh actions-lock extension for the GitHub CLI to generate .github/workflows/actions.lock for actions and their transitive dependencies. Adopt locking gradually: Onboard workflows individually. GitHub Actions requires each dependency of an onboarded workflow to be in the lockfile and runs its recorded commit. Keep updates in sync: When Dependabot opens a version update for an action in an onboarded workflow, it also regenerates the matching lockfile entry in the same pull request, without additional configuration. Require lockfile: Enterprise, organization, and repository administrators can use the Require lockfile policy to enforce adoption. Check for stale lockfiles: Verify that your lockfile is up to date without modifying files, including in a CI check. Lockfiles help protect against unexpected dependency changes, but they don’t determine whether a dependency is safe. Review dependencies before locking them. Get started Install the extension from the gh-actions-lock repository , then review and commit the generated lockfile and workflow changes. See workflow dependency lockfiles in GitHub Docs for details and setup instructions. Share feedback in the community discussion or report an issue with the extension . The post GitHub Actions workflow lockfiles are generally available appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

changelog.title: AI Scan for repositories in public preview
changelog.text: You can now use AI Scan to find vulnerabilities across your whole repository, not just in pull request changes. It covers languages and frameworks that CodeQL doesn’t support and finds issues that rule-based analysis can miss in languages CodeQL already covers. Findings appear in your GitHub code scanning alert list alongside CodeQL alerts. How it works Once your enterprise has enabled the AI Scan policy , organization owners and security managers can turn on AI Scan for repositories for their organization. For repositories owned by personal accounts, you turn it on in repository settings. This setting is separate from AI Scan for pull requests. After AI Scan for repositories is enabled, users with write access to code scanning can start a scan from the Code scanning page. Each scan analyzes the latest commit on the default branch. An agentic code scanner explores your repository and focuses on the code most likely to contain vulnerabilities. Each scan runs within a fixed time budget, which keeps its cost bounded. When both AI Scan and CodeQL are scanning the same repository, AI Scan skips issues that CodeQL already reports. On rescans, AI Scan keeps existing findings open if it detects them again and only reports new findings. Working with AI Scan alerts AI Scan alerts flow into the code scanning backlog just like other code scanning alerts and support the same workflows, such as assignees, linked pull requests, and issues. You can fix them with agentic autofix or add them to security campaigns. AI Scan alerts don’t automatically close when you merge a fix. Start a new scan after merging to check and close any alerts you’ve fixed. Availability AI Scan for repositories is available on github.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. A GitHub Copilot license isn’t required. Organization-owned repositories: Available for public repositories as well as for both private and internal repositories with GitHub Code Security or GitHub Advanced Security. Repositories owned by personal accounts: Available for public repositories. Private repositories owned by personal accounts aren’t supported. Billing AI Scan for repositories consumes Code Security AI credits. Usage appears in the “AI usage” section of enterprise billing and licensing under the “Advanced Security” product. You can set SKU-level budgets for Code Security AI credits, and if you’ve used up your budget, GitHub tells you before a scan starts. For public repositories owned by a personal account, usage is billed to that personal account, unless the repository owner has a GitHub Copilot license provided by an organization or enterprise. In that case, usage is billed to that organization or enterprise. Learn more about billing for GitHub Advanced Security AI features . Learn more about AI Scan and join the discussion in GitHub Community . The post AI Scan for repositories in public preview appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

changelog.title: Code scanning for AI applications in public preview
changelog.text: Code scanning can now detect AI applications and agent vulnerabilities, including indirect prompt injection (XPIA), sensitive information disclosure, excessive agency, and other AI-specific risks as coverage expands. Scans automatically run on pull requests. Here’s an overview of AI applications and agent vulnerabilities that are covered: Indirect prompt injection is the top risk in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications. It happens when malicious instructions are hidden in untrusted content (e.g., a file, webpage, or issue comment) that an AI agent reads. If that agent also has access to tools, data, or business systems, those hidden instructions can manipulate its behavior or trigger unintended actions. As more teams build agents into their codebases, these risky architectures can be difficult to spot through manual review alone. Sensitive information disclosure happens when an AI application or agent can access sensitive data without appropriate authorization controls, potentially exposing it to users or systems that should not have access. Excessive agency happens when an AI agent has more capabilities, permissions, or autonomy than its task requires, increasing the risk of unintended or high-impact actions. Code scanning for AI applications: Scans pull requests automatically when they’re created, alongside your existing CodeQL analysis. Flags agent code paths where untrusted content can reach a model that has access to tools, data, or business systems. Provides actionable mitigation guidance directly in the pull request so you can address the risk before it ships. If your organization uses GitHub Advanced Security, this detector starts scanning pull requests in repositories where code scanning and scans for AI applications are enabled. Review any new alerts on the Conversation or Files changed tab of your pull requests, and use the provided guidance to remediate before merging. Code scanning for AI applications is now in public preview on github.com and requires a GitHub Advanced Security license. It isn’t available on GitHub Enterprise Server at this time. Learn more about AI applications code scanning on pull requests and join the discussion in GitHub Community . The post Code scanning for AI applications in public preview appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

changelog.title: Push protection beyond predefined secret patterns
changelog.text: GitHub push protection is expanding beyond secrets with predefined formats. Developed in collaboration with Microsoft Applied Sciences, our new purpose-built classifier evaluates how potential secrets are used in surrounding code, allowing GitHub to block secrets even without a known and recognizable format. What’s new Starting today, you can enable push protection for AI-detected secrets for repositories with both push protection and AI-detected secret scans already enabled. The feature is available in public preview. Until now, push protection relied on predefined patterns to recognize secret types. Our new classifier introduces context-aware detection directly into the push path, allowing developers to catch and block more secrets before they enter repository history. Once enabled, it runs alongside pattern-based detectors, extending their coverage for new pushes, commits in the GitHub UI, and file uploads. If it detects a secret, GitHub rejects the change and reports the location of the secret. In early results, the classifier more than doubled the number of pushes where push protection caught a secret, with a user-reported precision rate rivaling that of issuer-defined detectors from our secret scanning partners. To resolve a block, remove the secret from every commit in the push and try again. Existing bypass and delegated bypass workflows still apply. Agents must get authorization before bypassing or working around a block. Availability and enablement The classifier is off by default in push protection. The feature can be enabled for repositories, organizations, enterprises, and enterprise-managed users. To enable the feature, a repository must have both AI-detected secrets and push protection already enabled. Repository admins can enable the feature from their repository settings page: Settings > Advanced Security > Secret Protection > AI-detected secrets > Block AI-detected secrets . Organization and enterprise admins can enable the feature from security configurations: Settings > Advanced Security > Security Configurations > Secret Protection > Secret scanning > AI-detected secrets > Block AI-detected secrets . Create or edit a custom security configuration with GitHub Secret Protection (GHSP) or GitHub Advanced Security (GHAS) and secret scanning enabled. Set each of the following settings to Enabled in the UI, or enabled through the security configurations REST API : UI setting REST API field AI-detected secrets secret_scanning_generic_secrets Push protection secret_scanning_push_protection Block AI-detected secrets secret_scanning_generic_secrets_push_protection Apply the configuration to the repositories you want to protect. The preview is available to organizations with GitHub Secret Protection or GitHub Advanced Security on github.com. AI detection in push protection consumes AI credits. Billing begins once you opt in to the public preview and enable the feature. AI-detected secret alerts from post-push scanning remain included with GHSP and GHAS at no additional charge. Learn more about secret scanning and push protection in our product documentation. The post Push protection beyond predefined secret patterns appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

changelog.title: Public monitoring for enterprises generally available
changelog.text: GitHub public monitoring alerts enterprises when their secrets are publicly exposed anywhere on GitHub, helping teams respond quickly to leaks wherever they happen. It’s now generally available to enterprises with GitHub Secret Protection at no additional cost. What is public monitoring? GitHub monitors the entire public surface of github.com for leaked secrets in real time. Public monitoring attributes those secrets back to your enterprise, based on where your people commit. Secret scanning has always protected the repositories you own, but secrets leak beyond that boundary. For example, a developer commits to a personal fork or an open source project or they paste a token into a public issue or pull request. This often happens from an account your security team isn’t tracking. Exposures like these were nearly impossible to find and often only surfaced after they’d been abused by bad actors. Public monitoring closes that gap. It finds these vulnerabilities and attributes them to your enterprise so you can respond quickly. The feature scans for secrets exposed anywhere in public content across github.com (e.g., git content, pull request comments, and user-created gists) and natively attributes each one back to your enterprise through GitHub’s identity layer and verified domains. Because the activity happens on GitHub, so does the attribution: in real time (not a nightly async crawl), definitively with native platform metadata (not on a guess from a commit email), and across arbitrary public repositories (not just surfaces where you tell us to look). Public monitoring will never scan private repositories; it surfaces only secrets that are already exposed publicly, so you can revoke leaked secrets before they’re abused by bad actors. Secret scanning for enterprises remains available for scanning all repositories owned by your organization or enterprise, including public, private, or internal repositories. Public monitoring works out of the box with no setup or configuration required. Just enable it and start seeing results. Why are we doing this? GitHub is committed to empowering the developer community by helping organizations recognize and address the risks of secret leaks wherever they happen. We believe every enterprise should know the moment its secrets leak in public, no matter where it happens on GitHub. That’s why public monitoring is now generally available for enterprises with GitHub Secret Protection, at no additional cost. Secrets don’t respect boundaries; scanning for them shouldn’t either. changelog.title: Prioritize Dependabot alerts with reachability analysis
changelog.text: Dependabot alerts can add up faster than a team can work through them. A vulnerable package in your dependency tree doesn’t always mean your code uses the vulnerable part of it, so knowing whether it does gives you more context when deciding where to start. Reachability analysis for Dependabot, now in public preview for JavaScript and TypeScript, adds that context to your alerts. It looks for call paths from your code to the vulnerable functions in your dependencies and shows the evidence on each alert. Use it alongside severity, EPSS score, production context, and your own knowledge of your application to prioritize and remediate dependency vulnerabilities in the way that works for your team. How it works Dependabot runs reachability analysis for you in a managed GitHub Actions workflow, so there’s nothing to install or maintain. For each advisory, the analysis uses curated data that identifies the vulnerable functions in the affected package. CodeQL builds a call graph across your repository and its dependencies, then searches it for a path from your code to each of those functions. Each open Dependabot alert gets one of these verdicts: Reachable: Your code has at least one call path to the vulnerable function. Potentially reachable: The analysis couldn’t determine whether your code calls the vulnerable function. Treat these alerts as reachable. Unreachable: The analysis completed and found no call path to the vulnerable function. These alerts are lower priority. Reachability unavailable: The alert couldn’t be analyzed. Triage it as you normally would. Verdicts appear on the Dependabot alerts you already use, and they never close or dismiss an alert. Filter and sort by verdict on the repository and organization alerts pages, or use the Dependabot alerts REST API to bring the same signal into your own tools and agents. Availability and requirements During the public preview: Cost: Free. You don’t need a GitHub Advanced Security license and you aren’t billed for the GitHub Actions minutes the analysis uses. Plans: GitHub Enterprise Cloud, including GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. Languages: JavaScript and TypeScript with an npm, Yarn, or pnpm lockfile in the repository. Runners: The analysis runs on GitHub-hosted runners. Self-hosted runners aren’t supported during the preview. As with Dependabot updates, you don’t need to turn on GitHub Actions for the analysis to run. Repository size and code complexity: Some monorepos and/or repositories with manifest files in multiple directories may not be supported during the preview. During the preview, if analysis runs for longer than three hours, some results might show “Reachability unavailable”. Advisory coverage: All GitHub-reviewed JavaScript advisories from the GitHub Advisory Database that receive Dependabot alerts are covered. Get started Reachability analysis is off by default. Turn it on for many repositories at once with a custom security configuration for your enterprise or organization, or for a single repository in the Dependabot section of Settings > Advanced Security . Dependabot alerts must be on to see reachability verdicts. The first scan starts right away and can take from a few minutes to a few hours. Scans then rerun daily while the repository has open Dependabot alerts, so verdicts keep up as your code and advisories change. To learn more, see About reachability analysis for Dependabot alerts in GitHub Docs. If you have questions or feedback, leave a comment in our Community discussion .
